prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, opening the 10^-18 regime of frequency metrology

statement.case_for: After reading all eight openings I move my preferred configuration to optical lattice clocks. It is the one candidate that colleagues with different specialities rank high (Kroll and Lindroth first, Pearce second, myself third), so the support does not rest on one member's field. It meets the 'discovery or invention' test cleanly: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice concept and first strontium demonstration, then Ye's drive to uncertainties near 1e-18. It is independently reproduced by many national laboratories, the interpretation is stable, and it is used in relativistic geodesy and in searches for varying constants. Credit fits two people with little truncation, which is a real advantage given how many other shortlisted cases (B017, B056, B015, B053) must drop important names to fit three.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty. Frequency metrology was honoured in 2005 (the comb) and in 2012 (control of single quantum systems), so some will see lattice clocks as an incremental step on prized ground. The redefinition of the second has not happened, and Katori and Ye share the field with Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto and others whom a two-name credit omits. Danielsson ranks it eighth, which I take as a fair signal that it is not a unanimous favourite. I also rank spherical-aberration correction (B055) first on my own ballot. It is a mature, original invention, but no other member ranks it and I cannot assess it neutrally from my own field, so I do not propose it as the preferred prize.

responses.point: Optical lattice clocks open a new frequency-metrology regime at 1e-18, are reproduced by many labs and are timely after the 2005 and 2012 prizes; a two-person prize is natural.
responses.response: I agree on the science and the two-name attribution. I am less comfortable calling the timing straightforward: the 2005 and 2012 prizes cover the comb and ion control, so the committee must be able to state what is new in the citation. I would write it around the neutral-atom magic-wavelength lattice and the resulting accuracy, not around precision metrology generally, which makes the distinction from earlier prizes explicit.

responses.point: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is a theory-plus-experiment case (Bistritzer-MacDonald flat bands, Jarillo-Herrero correlated insulators and superconductivity) that reshaped the study of correlation in 2D materials.
responses.response: I ranked it second and share your interest in the field, so this is a qualification rather than a rejection. The flat-band prediction and the 2018 experiments are a clean pairing, but the pairing mechanism is still unsettled and the discovery is under a decade old. I also worry that three names truncate a wider early history (Cory Dean, Philip Kim and others, plus earlier twisted-bilayer theory). I see it as a strong candidate for later, rather than this year ahead of a mature, settled achievement.

responses.point: Circuit QED is the architecture of superconducting quantum processors, with Schoelkopf, Wallraff and Girvin as a fair three-person split, and magic-angle graphene second but possibly somewhat early.
responses.response: Your own remark that twisted bilayer graphene may be early is the point I weight most, and it is why I rank it below the clocks. On circuit QED I agree on the importance but see a timing and attribution problem: the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits is recent, and the credited list has four people with Blais omitted from your trio, which is hard to justify for a proposal-and-experiment prize. I would want that resolved before ranking it above lattice clocks.

responses.point: The experimental Higgs discovery completes the 2013 theory prize, is very mature, and its credit rests on the founding spokespeople of ATLAS and CMS as a proxy for thousands.
responses.response: I agree the scientific case is exceptional and that recognition of the experimental side is arguably overdue. My difficulty is the one you flag yourself: naming Jenni, Della Negra and Virdee as proxies for two collaborations is an attribution judgement, and the prize is for the people responsible for the original work rather than for leadership of a large experiment. I cannot yet support it as the preferred prize, though I would keep it in view if the committee finds a defensible credit rule.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards optical lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Whether omitting Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto and other early lattice-clock contributors is acceptable in a two-name credit.
Whether magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is mature enough this year, given the unsettled pairing mechanism.
How to treat large-collaboration cases such as the Higgs discovery and IceCube under the three-person limit.
statement.conflict_note: I rank B055 (spherical-aberration correction) first on my own ballot and work in the same transmission electron microscopy community, with Chalmers colleagues and co-authors in microscopy, so I would recuse myself from any decision on B055 and do not use it as my preferred configuration. Göran Johansson is also at Chalmers, which should be noted when circuit QED (B017) is discussed. Otherwise my profile shows no specific connection to Katori, Ye or the other credited people on the shortlisted candidates.
